lec05kp11-u01-p12-nf-lec05-kp11-solution.name: fig:lec05-kp11-solution|Solution: Q1: s_C=½×8×0.5²=1, s_D=½×0.1×2²=0.2, so by the estimate remove D first; Q2: ρ(2)=2²/(2²+2²)=4/8=0.5, the weight is still 2 and only actually zeroing or removing it counts as deleting; check: a larger weight can have a smaller saliency.

lec05kp11-u01-p13-title.name: u01-p13-title
lec05kp11-u01-p13-title.text: Extension: the vector form, the derivative of the saturating penalty and a difference check

lec05kp11-u01-p13-bridge.name: u01-p13-bridge
lec05kp11-u01-p13-bridge.text: The weight is still 2 and a penalty value is not a deletion. How are the full Taylor conditions, the derivative of rho and a numerical check written out?

lec05kp11-u01-p13-c1.name: u01-p13-c1
lec05kp11-u01-p13-c1.text: **Vector Taylor form**: for weights $\mathbf w$ and a change $\delta\mathbf w$, $J(\mathbf w+\delta\mathbf w)-J(\mathbf w)\approx\nabla J(\mathbf w)^T\delta\mathbf w+\frac12\delta\mathbf w^TH\delta\mathbf w$; drop the first term only near a stationary point. The diagonal approximation is a shortcut; letting others compensate needs off-diagonal entries.

lec05kp11-u01-p13-c2.name: u01-p13-c2
lec05kp11-u01-p13-c2.text: **Derivative of the saturating penalty**: $\rho'(w)=\dfrac{2w(\tau^2+w^2)-w^2(2w)}{(\tau^2+w^2)^2}=\dfrac{2\tau^2w}{(\tau^2+w^2)^2}$. Weights are pulled toward zero; very large weights have a small derivative (saturated). Not the convex L1 penalty: no exact zero in finitely many updates.

lec05kp11-u01-p13-c3.name: u01-p13-c3
lec05kp11-u01-p13-c3.text: **Central difference check**: $H_{ii}\approx\dfrac{J(\mathbf w+h\mathbf e_i)-2J(\mathbf w)+J(\mathbf w-h\mathbf e_i)}{h^2}$. With $J(w)=(w-0.5)^2$, $w=0.5$, $h=0.1$ the costs are $0.01,0,0.01$, giving $(0.01-0+0.01)/0.01=2$, the analytic value. $h$ is the difference step, not the deletion threshold $\varepsilon$.

steps.label: Pruning, regularization and simulation evidence
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the lecture lec05-kp11 with view-from-text-v2: the pages were planned first (which figure covers which lecture sections) and each page is mainly one native infographic, with the terms defined inside the same figure. 9 main pages plus 4 extension pages (not timed). The scatter on page 8 is redrawn from the source's setup with the fixed seed 20261025: it is a sketch, not the source's original samples, and no network was retrained; the data setup, momentum parameters, 480 to 25 and the boundary change on pages 8 and 9 are the source's report and were not rerun. The lecture also has a supplementary p=0.5 contour demo that the deck omits. English version.

steps.label: Curvature and removal cost
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP11, following the network size of KP10. The question: a trained network may be redundant, so which connection should be removed, and is the weight size enough to tell? First three terms, in the cards on the right: pruning removes some connections or units and the result must still be checked; curvature is the second derivative, how fast the slope of the loss changes; the Hessian is the matrix of all second partial derivatives and its diagonal entries are the curvatures in each direction. On the chart the horizontal axis is the change δw, and removing a weight means δw equal to minus the weight. Red A: weight 0.2, curvature 100, a steep curve, removal cost one half times 100 times 0.2 squared, which is 2. Blue B: weight 1, curvature 0.02, a flat curve, cost one half times 0.02 times 1, which is 0.01. The curves are a local quadratic teaching sketch. Conclusion: the small weight A costs more to remove. The next page asks whether this cost can be estimated from the slope and the curvature before actually deleting.

steps.label: Deriving the saliency
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that the small weight A costs more to remove. This page asks whether the cost can be estimated without actually deleting. Four steps, top to bottom. Step 1, Taylor expansion: near a point, approximate the change of cost by the slope g and the curvature H, so delta J is about the sum of g times delta w plus one half the sum of H times delta w times delta w. Step 2: near a minimum g is about 0 and the first term vanishes. Step 3, the diagonal approximation drops the cross terms between different weights, leaving one half times the diagonal H times delta w squared. Step 4: removing means delta w equal to minus w, which gives the saliency s equal to one half H diagonal times w squared, an estimate of the removal cost. On the right, on a log scale: A, one half times 100 times 0.2 squared is 2; B, one half times 0.02 times 1 squared is 0.01; a factor of 200, so by the local estimate remove B first although its weight is larger. The four boxes below are the conditions: far from a minimum the first-order term may not be small, a large deletion makes higher-order terms matter, deleting several weights couples them, and with negative curvature a negative number must not be read as safe. The saliency is an estimate, not a measured loss. The next page asks how to put it into a pruning procedure that can be checked.

steps.label: The pruning procedure
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page derived the saliency, 2 for A and 0.01 for B. This page asks how to put the estimate into a procedure that can be checked. The saliency is not a measured value after deleting, so the procedure must include re-evaluation and retraining. Step 1: train to a suitable point. Step 2: estimate the saliency of every connection. Step 3: delete only a few of the lowest-saliency connections. Step 4: retrain what is left and check on validation data, then go back to step 2. Stop by validation performance, an allowed loss increase or a resource budget; the smaller network is not guaranteed to be more accurate every time. Methods with the full Hessian can also account for how other weights compensate, at the price of more storage and computation. The next page asks whether, instead of changing the structure, we can change the objective and add a model preference to the cost.

steps.label: Regularization
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page was the pruning procedure: estimate, delete a few, retrain and check on validation data. This page asks whether a model preference can be added to the cost from the start. Pruning changes the structure; regularization changes the objective first. Regularization adds a limit or preference on the model besides the data error: the total cost J total is the data error J data plus alpha times the weight penalty P, with alpha at least 0 setting the weight. Example with alpha equal to 0.1: model A has data error 0.10 and penalty P equal to 4, total 0.10 plus 0.1 times 4, which is 0.50; model B has data error 0.20 and P equal to 1, total 0.30; so B is chosen. On the right alpha is 0, only the data error counts, 0.10 is smaller than 0.20, and A is chosen instead. Note that this alpha is the penalty weight, not the momentum alpha; the data error as a sum or as an average has a different scale and then the same alpha acts differently, so it must not be copied across settings; alpha is chosen on validation data, and a smaller total cost does not guarantee a smaller test error. The next page asks which form the penalty P takes and why it does not push a weight straight to zero.

steps.label: Saturating penalty
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that the regularization alpha decides between A and B. This page asks which form the penalty P takes and why it does not push a weight straight to zero. The saturating penalty rho of w is w squared over tau squared plus w squared, with tau above 0 the scale; it approaches 1 for large weights, which is saturation; the total penalty P is the sum of rho over the weights. On the chart tau is 1: at w equal to 0.2, 1 and 3 it is about 0.0385, 0.5 and 0.9, marked by the green curve and three points. The orange curve is the derivative rho prime, which is 0 at w equal to 0, largest somewhere in the middle and small again later; so finite updates do not reach exactly zero. Weight elimination encourages shrinking during training and then periodically sets weights with absolute value below epsilon to zero or deletes them; epsilon is the deletion threshold, tau is the penalty scale, and the two serve different purposes. This is not the convex L1 penalty. The next page asks whether a single connection is enough, and how unit outputs and weight norms affect complexity.

steps.label: Three different operations
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that after the weights are squeezed, a threshold really deletes them. This page asks whether a single connection is enough. A connection is not a whole unit, and a unit is not a whole signal path. Column 1, delete a connection: set one weight to zero and check the data performance after deleting, because the saliency is only an estimate. Column 2, delete a unit: remove the unit with its connections and check the whole signal path, not one connection. Column 3, shrink a value: a weight or a unit output gets smaller but stays, and a small output may still be amplified by a large next-layer weight; the source also considers a penalty on neuron outputs to encourage smaller responses. Column 4 is the source's complexity term: for a two-layer sigmoid network under conditions such as a small training error and a bounded weight norm, it contains A cubed times the square root of log d over N, where A is a common bound on the summed absolute weights of each unit, d is the input dimension and N the sample count. With d and N fixed, doubling A makes this term 2 cubed, which is 8 times. This is only the source's order-of-magnitude summary, not a complete probability bound, and cannot be read directly as a classification error rate. The next page takes another route: start from a small architecture and add units one by one.

steps.label: Cascade correlation
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page said the three operations are recorded separately. This page takes another route: start from a small architecture, and ask how units are added one by one. First two terms. The residual is the true target minus the current prediction, e equal to t minus y hat, with n the sample index; cascade correlation adds one hidden unit that responds to the current residual and then retrains the output. Four steps: compute the residual; stage one trains the input side of the new unit so that the correlation score S between its output and the residual gets large, the new unit receiving the original inputs and the earlier hidden units; freeze the input-side weights of the new unit; stage two retrains the output side to reduce the squared error. The two stages must not be merged into one training objective. The teaching score S is the absolute value of the sum of products of the centred candidate output v and the centred residual e. With e equal to (−1, 1): the candidate v equal to (−1, 1) gives S equal to the absolute value of (−1)(−1) plus 1 times 1, which is 2; the constant candidate v equal to (1, 1) is all 0 after centring, so S is 0. This S is not divided by the standard deviations, so it is not the Pearson coefficient. The next page asks how the source verifies these methods in a simulation, starting with the data and network setup.

steps.label: The source's simulation setup
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page covered cascade correlation, where a new unit fills the residual. This page asks how the source verifies things in a simulation, starting with data and network. Data: class A has four means (0.4,0.9), (2.0,1.8), (2.3,2.3), (2.6,1.8); class B has (1.5,1.0), (1.9,1.0), (1.5,3.0), (3.3,2.6); each cluster has 50 points, so 8 times 50 is 400 points; each cluster has covariance 0.08 times the identity, so the standard deviation is the square root of 0.08, about 0.283, not 0.08. The scatter on the chart is redrawn from the same setup with the fixed seed 20261025: a sketch that only checks the distribution, not the source's original samples, and no network was retrained. The network is 2–3–2–1 with logistic activations, targets 1 and 0, and 9 plus 8 plus 3 equal to 20 parameters with biases. Momentum setting: mu 0.05 and alpha 0.85; adaptive momentum: mu 0.01, alpha 0.85, r i 1.05, c 1.05 and r d 0.7. Mu is the learning rate, alpha the momentum coefficient, r i and r d the factors that raise and lower the learning rate, and c the cost-ratio threshold that triggers lowering. The source reports that adaptive momentum is faster in batch mode. All of this is the source's report and was not rerun here. The next page asks what the pruning demonstration reported.

steps.label: The source's pruning report
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page was the source's simulation setup: eight clusters with 400 points and a 2–3–2–1 network. This page is the pruning demonstration. Two hidden layers of 20 units each; a model with 480 weights is trained first, the saliency is checked every 100 epochs, and finally 25 weights are kept. The remaining fraction is 25 over 480, about 0.0521, which is 5.21%; 455 are deleted, about 94.79%. The source reports better performance and a decision boundary that goes from curved to nearly straight; but this is a single case and cannot guarantee that pruning generally improves generalization. Limits to remember: the source does not fully explain how inputs, outputs and biases are counted, so a single architecture cannot be inferred and the inferred numbers must not be treated as facts of the source; the 400-sample 2–3–2–1 simulation and the 480-to-25 pruning demonstration are recorded separately and are not assumed to use the same data. All these numbers are the source's report; these experiments were not rerun here and the exact original curves are unavailable. The lecture also has a supplementary p equal to 0.5 contour demo that the deck omits. The next page returns to the saliency with an extension example.

steps.label: Extension: full second-order compensation
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page was the source's pruning report. This page is an extension that returns to the saliency: when other weights compensate, does the cost become smaller? This is a supplementary quadratic example, not a source experiment. The entries of H are H11 equal to 4, H12 equal to 1 and H22 equal to 2; deleting w1 equal to 0.5 means delta w1 equal to −0.5. Step 1, delete only w1 with delta w2 equal to 0: cost one half times 4 times 0.5 squared, which is 0.5. Step 2, let w2 compensate: delta J is 0.5 minus 0.5 times delta w2 plus delta w2 squared, and a cross term appears. Step 3, take the minimum: differentiating in delta w2 gives −0.5 plus 2 times delta w2 equal to 0, so delta w2 is 0.25 and the cost is 0.5 minus 0.125 plus 0.0625, which is 0.4375, below 0.5. The diagonal alone misses this effect; the off-diagonal H12 is needed. The next page has two exercises.

steps.label: Extension: exercises
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page showed that the cost can fall when other weights compensate. This page is the exercises. Exercise 1: C has weight 0.5 and curvature 8; D has weight 2 and curvature 0.1. By saliency, which is removed first? The hint is to compute s equal to H times w squared over 2. Exercise 2: take tau equal to 2 and w equal to 2 and compute rho of w. Does it mean the weight has been deleted? The hint is to tell a penalty from an actual operation. Work them out first; the next page is the worked solution.

steps.label: Extension: worked solution
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page set two exercises. Exercise 1: the saliency of C is one half times 8 times 0.5 squared, which is 1; the saliency of D is one half times 0.1 times 2 squared, which is 0.2; by the estimate D is removed first although its weight is much larger. Exercise 2: rho of 2 is 2 squared over 2 squared plus 2 squared, which is 4 over 8, which is 0.5. The weight is still 2, and only actually zeroing or removing it counts as deleting; the penalty value is only part of the cost. Check: a larger weight can have a smaller saliency. The next page is the last extension page: the vector form, the derivative and a numerical check.

steps.label: Extension: derivations and checks
steps.speakerNotes: The previous page's solution said a penalty value is not a deletion. This page writes out the formulas used so far. The first card is the vector form of the Taylor approximation: the first term can be dropped only near a stationary point, and the diagonal approximation is only a computational shortcut. The second is the derivative of the saturating penalty, obtained by the quotient rule as 2 tau squared w over the square of tau squared plus w squared; it is not the convex L1 penalty and does not guarantee exact zero in finitely many updates. The third is the central difference for when the second derivative is not computed directly: take J equal to the square of w minus 0.5, w equal to 0.5 and h equal to 0.1; the three costs are 0.01, 0 and 0.01 and the estimate is 2, equal to the analytic second derivative; h is a step, not the deletion threshold epsilon. This is the last page of KP11; the next KP asks whether many connections can share a few parameters from the start.
